passage:
In their Bengaluru flat, five-year-old Usha took a bite of banana and ran to put the rest on the little puja shelf for Ganesha. Ajji Nirmala caught her wrist gently. 'Not that one, kanda. Something you've bitten is jootha. God gets the first, fresh piece.'
Usha frowned. 'But I didn't bite much.'
Ajji smiled and gave her a whole banana to offer. At dinner, when Usha reached for Appa's steel tumbler, she stopped herself. 'Jootha,' she announced, and fetched her own. She still wasn't sure why. She only knew some things sat on one side of an invisible line.

qa.q: What did Ajji give Usha to offer?
qa.a: A whole banana.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when she frowned and said, 'But I didn't bite much'?
qa.a: She felt confused and a little disappointed, not understanding why her bitten banana wasn't good enough.

qa.q: How could Ajji help Usha understand the rule, not just follow it?
qa.a: Explain simply, when Usha asks, that offering the first, fresh piece is a way of showing care and respect, and answer her questions kindly.

qa.q: How might Ajji Nirmala feel seeing Usha fetch her own tumbler?
qa.a: Ajji may feel pleased and a little amused that Usha is already following the family custom on her own.

grounding: Shows a young child told not to offer bitten food at the shrine or drink from another's glass, who follows the jootha rule before understanding it.

passage:
'Zubin, don't drink from Manoj's glass, dikra. That's eththu.'
'What's eththu, Mamma?'
'Jootha. Once someone's lips touch it, it's theirs.'
'But Manoj is my best friend.'
'Even best friends get their own glass. Here.'
Manoj grinned. 'My Dadi says the same thing! Jootha!'
'Then why do you share your chocolate with me?'
'Because I break it first, silly.'
Zubin thought hard, then carefully broke his biscuit in two before offering half. 'Not eththu,' he told Mamma proudly.
'Very good,' Mamma said, trying not to laugh.

qa.q: What did Zubin break in two before offering it?
qa.a: His biscuit.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when he said 'Not eththu' to Mamma?
qa.a: He felt proud and pleased, happy to have followed the new rule correctly even without fully understanding it.

qa.q: How did Mamma handle Zubin's question in a helpful way?
qa.a: She gave a simple reason, offered his own glass, and praised his effort without mocking how literally he took the rule.

qa.q: How might Manoj feel hearing that Zubin's family has the same rule as his Dadi?
qa.a: Manoj seems happy and excited to find something in common, shouting 'Jootha!' with a grin.

grounding: Illustrates a young child learning not to drink from another's glass and to offer unbitten food, following the rule before understanding it.

passage:
"Ira! Don't drink from Bhaiya's glass," Mummy said. "It's jootha."
Ira, five, lowered the glass. "What's jootha?"
"Hemant bhaiya's mouth touched it. You use your own."
"But I love Bhaiya."
Hemant laughed. "It's not about love, pagli."
"Then what is it about?"
Mummy paused, wiping her hands. "It's just how we do it. Here, your own glass."
Ira took it. Then she looked at her half-eaten laddoo. "Can I give this to Ganesha?"
"No, beta. For God, only fresh, not bitten."
Ira nodded slowly and put the laddoo behind her back, as if it had done something wrong.

qa.q: Why did Mummy say Bhaiya's glass was jootha?
qa.a: Hemant bhaiya's mouth touched it.

qa.q: How does Ira seem to feel when she hides the bitten laddoo behind her back?
qa.a: Ira seems confused and a little guilty, sensing that bitten food is set apart though she doesn't understand why.

qa.q: How could Mummy explain jootha in a way Ira can grasp?
qa.a: Give a simple reason, like each person using their own glass and keeping fresh food for offerings, instead of 'it's just how we do it'.

qa.q: How might Hemant see Ira's 'But I love Bhaiya'?
qa.a: Hemant finds it funny and sweet, and gently tells her the rule isn't about love.

grounding: Shows a young child told not to drink from another's glass or offer bitten food to a deity, following the rule before understanding it.

passage:
Snack-time note, KG-B, Wednesday — Kavitha

Pankaj (5) has started saying "Jootha!" about everything. Today Aarohi held out half her sandwich to him, a big bite missing, and he jumped back as if it were hot. "No! Jootha!"

Aarohi's lip wobbled. She thought he meant she was dirty.

I asked Pankaj what jootha means. "Something bad. Mummy says don't take it." He didn't know why; he only knew the rule.

What I did next: I sat them together and explained that some families don't share bitten food, and that it doesn't mean anyone is dirty. Pankaj offered Aarohi an unbitten biscuit from his box. She took it.

qa.q: What did Aarohi hold out to Pankaj?
qa.a: Aarohi held out half her sandwich, a big bite missing.

qa.q: What does Pankaj's jumping back suggest about how he feels about bitten food?
qa.a: He seems alarmed, as if bitten food were dangerous, following a rule he doesn't understand yet.

qa.q: How did the teacher help both children?
qa.a: By explaining that some families don't share bitten food and that it doesn't mean anyone is dirty, then letting Pankaj offer an unbitten biscuit.

qa.q: How did Aarohi feel when Pankaj shouted 'Jootha'?
qa.a: Aarohi felt hurt, thinking he meant she was dirty.

grounding: Shows a young child following a rule about not taking bitten food before understanding it, and a teacher helping the friendship survive.

passage:
Under the guava tree behind the village school near Mathura, Nandini and Yusuf, both five, shared one guava: bite and pass, bite and pass.

On the way home Nandini stopped at the roadside shrine where Dadi lit a lamp each evening. She held the half-eaten guava up to the stone Hanuman. "For you!"

"Nahi, beti," Dadi said, gently catching her wrist. "For God, only what nobody has bitten. That one is jootha."

Nandini looked at the guava, then at Yusuf, puzzled. "But it's still good."

"Good for you two. For God, we give fresh." Dadi took a whole guava from her bag, and Nandini placed it very carefully.

qa.q: What did Nandini hold up to the stone Hanuman?
qa.a: She held up the half-eaten guava.

qa.q: Why was Nandini puzzled when Dadi called the guava jootha?
qa.a: Nandini felt confused, because to her a shared, bitten guava was still good; she follows the rule without yet understanding it.

qa.q: How did Dadi handle the moment gently?
qa.a: She caught Nandini's wrist softly, explained simply that offerings are fresh, and gave her a whole guava to place herself.

qa.q: How might Yusuf see the moment at the shrine?
qa.a: Yusuf may feel curious or puzzled too, since sharing the guava had been perfectly normal for them both.

grounding: Shows a young child learning that bitten food is not offered to a deity, and following the rule before understanding it.

passage: At the London park, Pablo held out his juice bottle to Tariq. "Want some?" Tariq, five, shook his head hard. "No! Jootha!" Pablo frowned. "What's jootha?" Tariq didn't know exactly. Nani said it about glasses you already drank from. "It's... not allowed." Pablo looked sad and put the bottle away. Tariq felt bad. At home he asked Nani why. She poured juice into two paper cups. "Now you can share." Next day, Tariq brought two cups.

qa.q: What did Tariq bring the next day?
qa.a: Two cups.

qa.q: How did Tariq feel after Pablo put the bottle away?
qa.a: He felt bad and a bit confused, following Nani's rule without really understanding it.

qa.q: How did Nani help Tariq keep the rule and still share?
qa.a: She poured juice into two separate cups, showing a way to share without drinking from one bottle.

qa.q: How might Pablo have felt when Tariq shouted "Jootha"?
qa.a: Pablo probably felt confused and hurt, not knowing why his friend refused.

grounding: It illustrates a child who follows a rule about not drinking from another's glass before understanding why.
